lesson.title: Straight Lines and Bell Curves: Reading a Normal Probability Plot
lesson.summary: Learn how plotting data against normal quantiles turns the question of whether data is normal into the question of whether a plot looks like a straight line, with a fully worked five-point example.
lesson.body:
Deciding whether a data set is approximately normal matters because so many statistical procedures, from certain confidence intervals to z-scores themselves, only behave the way theory promises when the underlying distribution is roughly normal. A histogram can suggest normality by looking bell-shaped and symmetric, which is the basic check inside assessing normality, but a histogram's shape can be deceiving depending on how wide the bars are drawn. The normal probability plot is a sharper tool: instead of asking whether a picture looks bell-shaped, it asks whether your data, plotted the right way, forms a straight line.

To build a normal probability plot, first sort the data from smallest to largest. Each ordered value gets a plotting position, an estimate of what percentile it occupies in the data set, commonly calculated as (i minus 0.5) divided by n, where i is the value's rank and n is the sample size. That percentile is then converted into the z-score a standard normal distribution would produce at that same percentile, sometimes called a normal quantile. Finally, you plot each data value against its normal quantile. The logic is direct: if the data really came from a normal distribution, the actual values and the values a normal distribution predicts at each percentile should rise together in a straight line. Curves, bends, and stray points reveal departures from normality.

Take five exam scores: 70, 75, 80, 85, 90, already sorted with n = 5. The plotting positions are (i minus 0.5) divided by 5 for i = 1 through 5, giving 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, and 0.90. The standard normal z-scores at those cumulative proportions are approximately -1.28, -0.52, 0, 0.52, and 1.28. Pairing each score with its normal quantile produces the points (-1.28, 70), (-0.52, 75), (0, 80), (0.52, 85), and (1.28, 90).

Plotting those five points shows a pattern that is close to a straight line but not perfectly straight, and that imperfection is instructive. The exam scores are evenly spaced by 5 points each, but the z-scores are not evenly spaced: the gap from -1.28 to -0.52 is 0.76, while the gap from -0.52 to 0 is only 0.52. Evenly spaced data does not produce evenly spaced z-scores, because the normal distribution is denser near its center and thinner in its tails. A truly normal data set compensates for this by spacing its middle values closer together than its extreme values, which is the gentle S-shaped spacing this small example is missing. Even so, five points this close to a line is generally read as consistent with approximate normality for a data set this small.

Systematic departures from a straight line are diagnostic. If the plot curves upward at both ends like the letter U, the data has lighter tails than a normal distribution, if it curves downward at both ends, the tails are heavier, meaning more extreme values than a normal model expects. A plot that curves in one direction overall signals skew. A single point sitting noticeably off the line is the normal probability plot's version of the outliers you learned to flag with the 1.5 times IQR rule, confirming the same unusual observation shows up whether you check for it with fences or with linearity.

This check is not just academic. Before trusting a confidence interval or hypothesis test that assumes normality, a careful statistician looks at the normal probability plot of the data because a badly curved plot is a warning that the normal-based formulas may not apply. Learning to read this plot now sets up nearly every inference procedure that follows in the course.
